I am thoroughly satisfied that if this House were composed for the main part of members of the medical profession, such pressure would be at once brought to bear upon the government as would result in prompt and effective action. There is no doubt whatever that the question is a very serious one to the people of Canada. The hon. gentleman who introduced the subject tells us, and tells us upon good authority, that this disease results in the death of about 8,000 of our people every year-more than twice as many as the number of men we sent to South Africa three or four years ago, and about four times or, perhaps, five times as many as the entire permanent military' force we maintain, including the Northwest Mounted Police. If there is any means by which parliament can minimize, or altogether stop, this scourge, it seems highly desirable that we should use it. My hon.. friend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) stated that the gentlemen interested in this question have placed no practical scheme before the House and the country. It seems to me that, if parliament has the power to deal with this question-and I think I shall be able to demonstrate, in a very few words, that it has-it is not for the government to sit idle on the treasury benches and wait for individual enterprise to place before them some scheme for dealing with this question ; but there is a duty and a responsibility placed upon the government themselves to take up this matter and deal with it promptly and in an effective way. The Minister of Agriculture seems to think that the government is in some way absolved from the duty of taking action in the matter, that they may sit silent and inactive for twenty or thirty years, perhaps, waiting for individuals to do that which the government ought to do. I do not take that view of the matter, unless it can be demonstrated that this government and this parliament have no right, and therefore no duty, Mr. FISHER.
to interfere. The Minister of Agriculture spoke of a section of the British North America Act-section 92. Well, that does not interfere at all with action by this parliament. In the first place, let me point out the resolution moved by my hon. friend from Argenteuil does not name the establishment of sanatoria. It is very simple and very general and, at the same time, very comprehensive :
That in the opinion of this House the time has arrived when parliament should take some active steps to lessen the widespread suffering and the great mortality among the people of Canada, caused by the various forms of tuberculosis.
Should the resolution be adopted by this House, it would be simply a request or, if you like, a direction to the government to seek out the remedy which best would abate this scourge, and which would be within the jurisdiction of this parliament. The clause of the British North America Act which the Minister of Agriculture called attention to was subsection 7 of section 92. This subsection gives, as one of the subjects confided to the exclusive jurisdiction of the legislatures of the provinces :
The establishment, maintenance and management of hospitals, asylums, charities and eleemosynary institutions in and for the- province, other than marine hospitals.
Now, even if the view which the Minister of Agriculture seems inclined to take were the correct view, we could act in this matter in any one of three ways. The Dominion authority could gather information and diffuse literature on this subject. It could create a criminal jurisprudence in connection with the subject, if it thought fit or necessary ; or, as has been well pointed out by more than one member of the House in this debate, it could give financial aid. The Minister of Agriculture does not seem to realize how much this parliament and this government have aided matters which are of purely provincial interest, if you look merely at the scope of the British North America Act. For example, the Minister of Agriculture says it is not desirable for parliament to interfere by granting financial aid in connection with work to be done by the provinces, that it would be better, as I understood him, to leave such matters entirely to the jurisdiction of the provincial legislatures. Does not the Minister of Agriculture remember that, during the past eight years, as well as before that time, we have interfered by assisting local enterprises in the shape of provincial railways, which are as much subject to the jurisdiction of the provinces as the establishment of sanatoria for the purpose of abating the ravages of this consumption. Almost every session since 1890 we have had aid granted by the parliament of Canada to local railways, provincial railways, which have not been declared works for the general advantage of Canada.
And inland navigation.

Yes, and inland navigation also, as my hon. friend from Victoria (Mr. Sam. Hughes) points out. 1 give these merely as illustrations ; hut, by looking over the estimates for the previous years, many illustrations could be found quite as forcible as those to which I have called attention. Therefore, there seems no good reason why, if the ravages of this disease are as extensive and as much to be dreaded as the hon. gentlemen have stated who have addressed the House, there is no good reason why parliament should not interfere. We have had royal commissions on various questions in the past on matters of very much less importance to the country as a whole than that which has engaged the attention of the House this afternoon. If the government have any doubt as to the extent of the evil that has been spoken of, or any doubt as to the best means of deal ing with the evil, a short but thorough and comprehensive inquiry might be made by some such means as I have pointed out. In that way action on the part of the government might be expedited.
I rose more for the purpose of expressing my view, given without very much consideration, because I did not intend to speak, that, under the British North America Act, there is scope for this government and parliament to deal with the question. The parliament of Canada has a right under section 91 of the British North America Act, to make laws for the peace, order and good government of Canada. And, while the construction which, at one time, was placed upon these words has been supposed to be narrowed by a decision given not long ago in the Privy Council, I think that if we look at the whole scope of the authorities, including that which I have just mentioned, we can come to the conclusion that the parliament of Canada need not hold its hand in this matter for want of jurisdiction over this question. In a very well known work on the constitution of Canada, the work of Mr. Lefroy on legislative power in Canada, a work well known to all lawyers, and one that has been spoken of by the Minister of Justice in this House as one of the very best works that have ever been written on this subject, at page 384, the language of Lord Herschell is quoted :
A sanitary regulation might be passed by a local legislature, but that would not prevent a general sanitary regulation of a similar nature necessary for the safety of the whole Dominion being enacted by parliament.
Further on, quoting again the language of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, and dealing with the very clause of the British North America Act to which I have referred, I find the following :
Laws of this nature designed for the promotion of public order, safety or morals, and which subject those who contravene them to criminal 444
procedure and punishment belong to the subject of public wrongs rather than to that of civil rights.
But there is even more direct authority in the very case to which I have just referred, the case of the Attorney General, of Canada against the Attorney General of Ontario, in which the validiy of the Liquor License Act for the province of Ontario was questioned before the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. During the argument in that case Lord Herschell used the following very significant language :
Take sanitation for example, suppose that the Dominion parliament had, with a view to the health of the whole Dominion, passed certain regulations, and supposing in a particular province a particular disease was raging which rendered it necessary for the safety of all those within the province that much more stringent regulations as to the inhabitants of the houses should come into force. Should not that he considered a merely local matter. ? If it is so, it is intended to be dealt with, and you limit your regulations to the locality ; and why is that inconsistent if the legislation is on the same lines as that which is in force in the Dominion at large ?
You will perceive, Sir, that Lord Herschell concedes the right of the parliament of Canada to make general sanitary regulations applicable to the whole Dominion, and at the same time he holds that, consistently with that federal jurisdiction, it might be possible for a local legislature, acting within its jurisdiction, to deal with the question of sanitary regulation purely from a local and provincial standpoint and with regard to a particular emergency which may have arisen in any province. Further than that, the very ease to which I have just referred-and it is a case wherein , it was supposed that the jurisdiction of this parliament was limited under the words of clause 91 of the British North America Act-even in that case you will find direct authority for the proposition which I have endeavoured to present in a very few words. The lieadnote or synopsis of that case is as follows, as far as this particular question is concerned :-
The general power of legislation conferred upon the Dominion parliament by section 91 of the British North America Act of 1867, in supplement of its therein enumerated powers, must be strictly confined to such matters as are of unquestionable national interest and importance, and must not trench on any of the subjects enumerated in section 92 as being within the scope of provincial legislation, unless they have attained such dimensions as to affect the body politic of the Dominion.
If the statements of fact made this afternoon, and supported by the best authority, are correct, then it is impossible to deny that this is a question of national interest and importance and one which has attained such dimensions as to affect the body politic of the whole Dominion. Therefore under these circumstances and in view of

these and other authorities which might he cited, 1 for one have no doubt that means might be found and a measure devised by which parliament could deal with this subject and deal with it effectively in the interests of the whole Dominion.

I shall not, Mr. Speaker, take up the time of the House for more than a few minutes. Most of the remarks made this afternoon were on the line of the government doing something by way of encouraging the maintenance and establishment of sanatoria. While I have no desire to say a word in disparagement of such a course, while I think that much may be done by means of sanatoria in preventing contagion and adopting methods of cure that may be practised within the institution itself, I think a great deal more can be done by means of education. No matter what the government may do for the establishment of sanitoria, there will always be throughout this country many men and women who will not be able to take advantage of these institutions. There must be many men and women who will have to continue to be bread winners as long as they are able to work, and to whom it will be an impossibility to leave their homes and their work and become inmates of these institutions. I remember that in the town in which I live some citizens became possessed of a pamphlet on this dread disease of consumption, and so great was the interest it excited that the pamphlet was passed from one to another and I think a great deal of benefit resulted. Therefore it seems to me that the distribution if literature and the impressing upon the minds of the people the fact that consumption is not hereditary but exceedingly contagious, and that there are methods which may be used in the ordinary homes by the ordinary householders that will lead to its cure, especially if practised in the early stages, and that there are likewise methods which may be used by the ordinary householder to prevent the spread of the contagion, is of great importance and that the information/ thus given cannot fail to result in a great deal of good. With that end in view, I think the suggestion an exceedingly good one that a commission be appointed by this House to gather all possible information on the subject. The report of such a commission would prove a splendid literature for circulation and distribution among the people and would contain no doubt much information regarding the means which the government might take to combat this dreaded scourge.

If there is no one else to address the House on this subject. I would like to say a few words in winding up the debate. I have very little to add to what has been said by those hon. gentlemen who spoke this afternoon. I was very glad to hear my hon. friend the Min-Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
ister of Agriculture express himself in favour of having something done in this matter, but of course one might naturally expect this of the hon. gentleman who has been a member of the executive committee ever since its formation and has always taken great interest in the work. I am sure that not one of us wishes to have anything done which would be in contravention of the British North America Act, and I was pleased to see my hon. friend the leader of the opposition put the case as he did, as it certainly confirms my view. I do not agree with the Minister of Agriculture, that there is a well defined division in the British North America Act with regard to this matter. There are many matters concerning the public health which are not referred to in that Act at all, and concerning which both the Dominion and the provinces have the right to legislate. In the Department of Agriculture itself, I have noticed that on one of the doors, not far from the minister's office, there is the inscription * Director of Public Health ' which must mean something. That must have been put there for some purpose, and the office, I may say, is occupied by a gentleman well qualified to fill it. In the Quarantine and Health Act, chapter 63 of the statutes of 1868, to which I referred this afternoon, you will find in clause seven a distinct reference to public health, and that great powers in that respect were assumed by this parliament. It reads as follows :-
Whenever Canada or any part thereof appears to be threatened with any epidemic, endemic contagious or infectious disease the Governor may by proclamation make such regulations as he thinks proper and necessary to prevent the introduction of such disease from beyond the limits, or to prevent its spread within the limits of Canada, and otherwise protect the public healthy and he may, from time to time, revoke or amend i he same, or make others in their stead in like manner, and may impose penalties, forfeitures and punishments for the breach thereof, and such regulations shall be published at least twice in the ' Canada Gazette,' and the production of copies of the ' Gazette ' containing such proclamation, shall be evidence of the making, date and contents of such regulations.
This Act was in force from 1868 to 1872, when it was repealed at the instance of the Minister of Agriculture because he objected io paying the expense of carrying it out. But if that Act was legal in 1808, surely a similar Act will be legal now. If it were in contravention of the British North America Act in 1868, surely it would have been objected to, more especially as the British North America Act was fresh in the minds of the members of parliament of that day, among whom were the fathers of confederation. I therefore contend that while technically sanatoria are placed by the British North America Act in the hands of the provinces, the question of public health is not so placed.

Now I may say that this resolution of mine is general in its terms. I do not ask especially for sanatoria, but the association thought this was the best way to start the fight against this disease. At the same time they have no set plan, they ask for no special thing. We simply come before this parliament with this resolution, and if it is passed I will take it as a request to the government to appoint a commission, or to adopt some means to find out in what way this parliament may help to stop the spread of this disease and the great number of deaths caused by it, without in any way contravening the British North America Act.

There can be no objection whatever to the passage of the resolution. I think that the discussion itself will have a very beneficial effect in attracting public attention to a subject that so seriously , affects every household in the Dominion or Canada. There has been much light thrown upon the dreadful white plague within the last few years. Since the discoveries or the researches of Prof. Koch and his school of German scholars, the public have come to learn the first elements in connection witB the prevention of the disease. Until a recent date it was regarded as hereditary ; that theory appears to have given away to another one now, one that is better founded, and I think pretty well established in that by acting upon it there has been a great dimunition in the spread of this scourage. I had not the advantage, Mr. Speaker, of hearing the early part of the discussion, but I do not understand from the few explanations the Minister of Agriculture has given me of it, that he for a moment takes the ground that the Dominion government has not jurisdiction to some extent. It might be possible, by some species of technicality, to oust our jurisdiction in some ways, but still there are methods that every legislature and every community in Canada may take, each contributing within its sphere towards the abatement, and we will hope ultimately the extirpation of this great danger to human life. This subject, education, and the dissemination of information, is one clearly within the jurisdiction of every parliament. There can be nothing in any constitution that will prevent this parliament, or any parliament, or any legislative body, municipal or otherwise, from contributing towards enlightening the people how they may best prevent the extension and spread of the disease, and perhaps with more or less success confine the disease where it has acquired a foothold. I think I am safe in making the pledge on behalf of this government, that whatever we can do in aid of the very meritorious object of this resolution, will be done.
Motion agreed to.

McLEAN moved for :
Copies of all correspondence, telegrams, reports, writings, documents, memorials, Orders in Council, memorandum, or written or printed information of any kind not already down, which passed between the government of Canada, or of any minister or official thereof, in any wise relating to the claim of the province of Prince Edward Island to a share of the Halifax fishery award.
He said :	In making this motion, I desire to make a short statement. I noticed that in the speech from the Throne delivered by the Lieutenant Governor of Prince Edward Island at the opening of the session in 1903, it was stated that negotiations were then in progress with a view to settling this vexed question of the distribution of the Halifax fishery award. It was stated by the leader of the government of the province of Prince -Edward Island that a conference had taken place in Ottawa between the premiers of New Brunswick, Quebec and Prince Edward Island, at which the Minister of Justice of the Dominion of Canada was present, and that it was settled at that time that the question should be submitted to the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada. The question came before the legislature during the session of 1903, and the premier of the province stated that negotiations with reference to the submission of the matter to the Supreme Court of Canada had been for some reason abandoned, and that negotiations were going on with a view to having the matter submitted to the decision of the Privy Council in England. It seems that though this took place some eighteen months ago. nothing, so far as the people of the maritime provinces know, has taken place since. I think it would be very interesting to the people of the maritime provinces, and to the others interested in the distribution of this award, to know what the negotiations are and how they stand to-day, and when, if at all, the distribution of this large amount will take place.

Mr. BOYCE moved for :
Copies of all correspondence and documents relating to an application to the Board of Railway Commissioners, and relating to an application lately before the said board, by the towns of Port Arthur and Fort William, to obtain access for their municipal telephone system into the offices of the stations of the Canadian Pacific Railway in the two towns. And for copies of all correspondence between the said towns of Port Arthur and Fort William, and the officers thereof, with the government, with reference to such application, or prior or subsequent thereto. Also copies of any report or recommendation, decision or order made by the Railway Commissioners with reference to
suclx application or applications, or incident thereto.

Before that motion is carried 1 wish to refer for a moment to an incident that occurred within the last few days on this very question. The Prime Minister then made the statement that he thought well of introducing a General Act dealing with the telephone question in this country, and his attention at that time was called to this very substantial grievance in connection with the use of telephones in the towns of Port Arthur and Fort William. It has been pointed out in this House time after time that the decision, so far as the country is concerned, is a very interesting one, and that while the former Minister of Railways put a clause in the Railway Act compelling railroad companies to give access in their stations to all telephone companies, that Act was interpreted by the then chairman of the Railway Commission to mean that the compensation to be paid railways and to railway companies was of a general character and that they were entitled to large damages if such a thing took place.
Now, my belief is that the claim cannot be justified, that this contract, as it exists between the Bell Telephone Company and the railway companies, is against the public interest, is against the provisions of the Railway Act and if investigated by the govern-meiit or in the courts, or if it were referred to the Supreme Court, it would be declared to be unconstitutional and against the public interest. Time after time this question has come up. The then Minister of Railways and Canals, when he passed his Railway Act and when he put that provision into the Act which secured telephonic entrance into all stations for all companies, said that the object desired at that time would be secured. It was not secured, but the then Minister of Railways and Canals went upon the Railway Commission as chairman of that commission and he interpreted that Act, as far as I can read his judgment, as against the public interest, as in the interest of the Bell Telephone Company, and although that decision wras given months and months ago, nothing has been done to ascertain the rights of the public in this matter. Day after day we are passing legislation in this House in the interest of the three great railway companies who are parties to that contract which is against the public interest. I say it is the duty of the government not only to remedy the grievance, not only to make it clear in the Railway Act that this relief should be afforded, but that we should say to these railway companies : Until you grant the public the remedy of the grievance complained of in this matter we refuse to give you any legislation that you desire. East year the Grand Trunk Railway Company was given the greatest franchise that was ever given in this country. The Canadian Pacific Railway, every session of this parlia-Mr. BOYCE.
ment, is given franchises and concessions of various kinds, and the only thing to be done on the part of the government, if they are interested in the public welfare, is to say to these railway corporations : Not one thing more will you get from this House or from this government until you remedy that grievance. But, the companies get more legislation and the grievance complained of is not remedied. This matter will come up later on in this session and it may come up during this very week, but again I point out that the cure of this grievance complained of is in the hands of the government, that they can cure it by legislation and they are bound to do it, they can cure it by negotiation with the companies or they can cure it by passing an Act declaring that such contracts are against the public interest. Then, for a moment let us recall what this contract involves. The Canadian Pacific Railway which had immense subsidies in money and immense grants of land from the people and great franchises, and the Grant Trunk Railway Company, which had the same from the people of this country and which only within the last two years got the greatest franchise that was ever given by this country, make a contract with the Bell Telephone Company that no independent telephone company shall have access to any railway station unless it be the Bell Telephone Company. My hon. friend from Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) pointed out the other day how far this thing was carried. In this county there is no Bell Telephone service given to the people, but so strong is the Bell Telephone Company under this contract that they say that the independent company shall not have a connection with the railway station. In Port Arthur and Fort William they have a splendid municipal telephone service. That telephone service is refused access to the Canadian Pacific Railway station and the Canadian Northern station, and yet the people of Port Arthur and Fort William are the main customers in those towns of both those railways. They are the people who do business with the railways, the people who travel over the railways the people who furnish and receive freight from these railways, and yet by reason of this iniquitous, agreement, this agreement which is contrary to public policy and which should be declared to be contrary to public policy if the government were alive to their responsibilities is allowed to continue. For two years now this thing has continued. For two years attempts have been made to direct the attention of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Emmerson) to this iniquitous agreement but so far he has had nothing to say on the question. So far he has not facilitated ,the consideration of the question by the Supreme Court as the law provides but he has allowed it to drag along and that is the position of the question to-day. Surely the government have enough courage, surely they have a sufficiently high conception of their duty
*4

to the people to tell these railway companies that if they do not cancel that contract the government will find a way of passing a law to abolish it. But. so far they have done nothing in that direction. What is the strength of the Bell Telephone Company in this country that they are allowed to maintain a monopoly of that kind ? I do not know what is the cause of the influence that they seem to have, hut every proposition that was made during the discussion of the Railway Act that seemed to tread on the corns of the Bell Telephone monopoly was objected to, no attention is paid to the demand for redress of the grievance which is now complained of, and the Bell Telephone monopoly is allowed to ride roughshod not only over the rights of the people but over the rights of municipalities and provinces. The responsibility must rest with the administration of the day to And a cure for the existing state of things. It is all very well to tell the people at Port Arthur, Fort William, Locust Hill and Labelle to go to the courts and maintain their rights but their is an easy way to correct this grievance and that way" is for the government to exercise the power that undoubtedly rests in them of declaring the contract to be against public interest, to rescind the Act if necessary and compel the company to treat every one justly. As I pointed out in the House the other day in connection wuth this subject the Bell Telephone Company was incorporated in this country for the public interest, and any company incorporated for the public interest is bound to treat every section of the community fairly and equitably. They do not treat every one equitably. They only allow Bell Telephone customers to have access to the railway stations. In two ways this grievance can be remedied immediately. It can be remedied immediately by a change in the Railway Act and it can be remedied by a general law in so far as this parliament has control over corporations created by this parliament. Again I ask the government : Why is this remedy denied ? Why have they not courage to rectify this grievance? Is it that the men who are identified with the Bell Telephone Company are warm political friends of theirs ? The only explanation I can arrive at after all that has taken place is that in some way political friendship has more control here than has the public interest, and I ask hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House why it is that this grievance of two years standing is not rectified and why we have to make motions of this kind, why we have to go to the courts and make motions of another kind when the power to remedy this grievance is in the hands of the government.

Mr. Speaker, 1 understand that the Railway Act has referred to the Railway Commision the determination of a question of this kind. I do not think any lawyer will say that the commissioners have not power to deal with
this question. This is a motion respecting the Bell Telephone Company in two towns and a question arising under somewhat exclusive powers given by the Canadian Pacific Railway, I believe, to the Bell Telephone Company at these points. The matter came before the Board of Railway Commissioners after having heard evidence they gave judgment declaring that the exclusive privilege should come to an end, and that the only question remaining to be determined was that of compensation. I am not aware that the parties to the litigation, if we may so describe the nature of the strife, have since brought the subject before the commissioners.

When was that judgment
given ?

I believe it was given about last July. I do not remember exactly, but I remember reading the opinion of each commissioner. The result of their finding was that they would not yield to the contention of the Bell Telephone Company that it could exclude other lines from access to the Canadian Pacific Railway and they declined to allow the Canadian Pacific Railway to shelter itself behind the special contract made with the Bell Telephone Company and exclude other companies from access to their station. The question, therefore, simply became one of compensation, as to whether the applying company should pay compensation, not only for installing their wires, but also the damage for a breach of contract. That is the great question involved. I do not understand that any of the commissioners have expressed any opinion on that point. They have simply affirmed that it is a question of compensation, and if the parties desire to have an opinion and would prosecute the inquiry, then they would get a judgment from the commissioners as to their view of the law, as to whether or not in their judgment the company, the Canadian Pacific or the Bell Telephone Company, was entitled to any consequential damages by reason of the setting aside of this contract. I think that before we commence to amend laws we should try to find out what they mean by the proper tribunal and there is a proper tribunal to-day to determine the question. Of course we cannot prevent people, making such suggestions as have fallen from the lips of the hon. member for South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean) ; I can only say that I am quite satisfied that there is no foundation for his suspicions whatever. We have, we think, vested the subject in an independent and competent tribunal, composed of three gentlemen who I believe are in no way biased by considerations towards any of the parties interested but are influenced only by a high consideration of public duty and high regard for the law. If that question, therefore, were threshed out, and we had a decision either from that tribunal or from the Supreme Court,-for the parties

have a right to appeal to the Supreme Court, -then parliament would know whether or not the present legislation was adequate to meet the situation, and if it was not, parliament would then be in a position to consider what would be proper amendments to the law.

I can assure the hon. Postmaster General (Sir William Mulock) that I am not indulging in satire when I say that the House must be indebted to him for his explanation of this all-important question, and I must express my regret that the Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. H. R. Emmerson) was not so well informed, so anxious or so willing to give information, as the minister who has given the explanation to-night. The next question was :
Did the Board of Railway Commissioners decide that' the Canadian Pacific Railway must Sir WILLIAM MULOCK.
allow the municipal telephone system in Port Arthur and Fort William to be connected with the railway stations on the payment of compensation ? If so, has the order been carried out ?

Will my hon. friend give the date on which he asked the question ?

On the 6th of February on page 595 of Hansard. I think it is due to this House that the hon Minister of Railways should now explain how it was that on that date lie could not or would not give a defi-inite answer to these questions, while he has given the information with which he has

favoured this House to-night, showing that it was within his power to obtain the answers and they were within his personal knowledge. But there is in question something to which my hon. friend from South York referred the other day, and which may have occasioned the hon. minister some little difficulty, that is, the question of the rights of municipalities in this important matter- a question on which the hon. gentleman perhaps thought there was a little danger of committing the government either to one policy or the other, and as to which he was treading on somewhat dangerous ground. The municipalities, as the hon. gentleman perhaps knows, and as perhaps he knew when these questions were before him, are and have been awaiting a decision of these important questions. It is of the utmost importance that the municipalities should be informed with regard to what their rights are, and if the facts be, as shown by the hon. member for South York, that in this case as in other cases the franchise granted to the Bell Telephone Company has enabled it to exclude municipal franchises and to trample on the rights of other corporations and individuals, the sooner that state of affairs is put an end to the better it will be for the liberties of the people.

Mr. Speaker, I do not know that in answering the question put by my hon. friend on February 6 I did not cover all the points mentioned in that question. My hon. friend, if I am to judge by his tone and attitude in this House, would never confess that he lacked any information or that he was unable to answer any question that might be put to him. I invite the attention of the House to the question:
What is the present status of the application now before the Board of Railway Commissioners of the town of Port Arthur and Fort William, to get access for their municipal telephone system into the Canadian Pacific Railway stations in the two towns ?
My hon. friend, I understand, is a lawyer, and I am sure that he will recognize that there is a question of law. He must bear in mind that it was the subject matter of litigation before the Railway Commission, that the commission had delivered a judgment in respect to it, and, therefore, the best information that could be given to this House and the country in regard to it would be a return of the judgment delivered by that tribunal. My hon. friend the Postmaster General has given his opinion with respect to this case, but my hon. friend did not for a moment contend that he was giving more than his own interpretation of the judgment delivered by that court. The next question was :
Did the Board of Railway Commissioners decide that the Canadian Pacific Railway must allow the municipal telephone system in Port Arthur and Fort William to be connected with the railway stations on the payment of compensation ?
That is a question that can only be fully and amply answered by a recital of the judgment. I could have brought to this House the judgment, and I could have read it, but that would not have been a proper answer; that is not the ordinary way ot answering these questions. My hon.; friend might very well have read it himself. The whole question could be best answered by a return of the papers, which are in the possession of the Board of Railway Commissioners. They are not in the Department of Railways and have no connection with that department. What is the present status of the application now before the Board of Railway Commissioners

Bill (No. 59) to amend the Act respecting the jurisdiction of the Exchequer Court as to Railway Debts-Mr. Geoffrion-was read the second time, and House went into committee on the Bill.
Mr., FISHER.
I think we ought to have some explanation as to why this is necessary and whether it would be advisable to make it of general application. What is the particular object ?
Does the hon. gentleman (Mr. R. L. Borden) wish to know why it is proposed to apply it only to the province of Quebec?
Yes.

It is because that (provision was placed in the old Insolvent Act and Winding Up Act. I understand that the other provinces do not care about having this inserted, because they have a different system ; but in the province of Quebec there is the difficulty that only judicial sales made by the sheriff clear immovable property from all incumbrances. For instance, in the old Insolvent Act such a provision was inserted. In cbhpter 16, section 76, 38 Vic., 1875, there is this provision :
All sales of real estate made by the assignee shall vest in the purchasers all the legal and equitable estates of the insolvent therein, and the conveyance may be in the form ' N ' ; but in the province of Quebec such sale shall, in all respects, have the same effect as to mortgages, hypothecs or privileges then existing thereon, as if the same had been made by a sheriff under a writ of execution issued 1 in the ordinary course, but shall have no other greater or less effect than such sheriff's sale, and in the province of Quebec the title conveyed by such sale shall have no equal validity with a title created by a sheriff's sale.
Now we passed an Act in 1903 giving jurisdiction to the Exchequer Court, in case of the insolvency of a railway, to put it in the hands of a receiver, who may proceed to sell it. But when we came to apply that law in the province of Quebec to the Quebec Southern road, and the road was put up for sale, nobody would buy it, because a clear title could not be given. This was clearly an oversight in the law of 1903, and by this Bill I wish to give to a sale made by the Exchequer Court, the very same effect as a sale by a sheriff in the province of Quebec, and to apply the same principle as was applied in the old Insolvency Act and the Winding Up Act. I think the members of this House will see the necessity of amending the Act in the way I have pointed out; particularly is there a necessity for this amendment in the province of Quebec. But I have no objection to make it applicable to all the provinces, although another system seems to prevail in the other provinces. But I have no objection to amend it so that it will apply to all the provinces. In any case, I desire to provide that a sale made by the Exchequer Court shall convey the same guarantee and the same title as a sale made by a sheriff in the province of Quebec.

Of course it is highly desirable that any title obtained under a judicial sale such as this should be a good title, or at least that any one purchasing should know exactly what he is purchasing. I am not at all suggesting that some amendment to the law should not be made ; but if the Act is defective so far as the province of Quebec is concerned,
I do not see how it can be absolutely effective so far as the other provinces are concerned. It is the practice in Nova Scotia, for the most part, to have judicial sales conducted by Sheriffs under the direction of the court, and that practice, as I understand, prevails in the province of Quebec ; in the province of Ontario, I think it is different; there judicial sales, at least sales under mortgage, and I suppose all judicial sales are conducted by the master in chancery.
By any officer appointed for the purpose.
In New Brunswick it is by a referee in equity.

Well, I think we should have the same general legislation making such sales legal in all the provinces, and we should have some provision, either in this Act or by means of power given to the judge of the Exchequer Court, to make rules, if that is not already in existence, so that we may have the same uniform practice throughout the whole country. I would think it undesirable for courts of this character, having jurisdiction in every province in Canada, to have one practice in one province and another practice in another province ; except of course in so far as such variation may be absolutely necessary in consequence of the different systems of jurisprudence which prevail in this country.

While the control of the Halifax and Esquimau garrisons will pass into the hands of Canada on July 1, the Dominion will only take over the different services gradually. There is certain work with which Canadians are not yet familiar, and British officers and men will continue in such positions until 'Canadians qualify. Canada could supply the necessary infantry in short order, hut it would take some time to get an engineering staff, &c.
Canada regards with great favour the compliment which Britain has paid her in handing over these important defences to her care. The trust will be well looked after. Great credit is due Lord Grey for the interest he has taken in carrying these negotiations to a speedy and satisfactory conclusion.
It will be remembered that during the colonial conference Sir Frederick Borden made an offer to take over Halifax and Esquimau defences. Canada is prepared to pay every dollar that is required for Canadian defences on Canadian soil.
I do not know whether this article is inspired or not, especially the last clause of it, where it speaks of Canadian defences on Canadian soil. As far as I am personally concerned, I hope the statement is not true. I would be very sorry that Great Britain should so far forget her duties to the empire as to surrender Halifax and Esquimalt; and, secondly, I hope that if Canada is to contribute to Imperial defence -and I trust at no far distant day she will -in place of garrisoning Halifax and Esquimau, she may be found garrisoning Portsmouth, Gibraltar, Malta and other places, and we will contribute our fair share towards the defence of the empire. I notified the hon. minister that I would bring this up, and I would be pleased to receive his statement.

Mr. Speaker, I may say at once to my hon. friend (Mr. Sam. Hughes), and to the House, that the article which he has read was not inspired by the government, nor by any member of it, so far as I know ; in fact, it was an entirely unauthorized publication. However, it may be a convenient opportunity at this moment to state what has happened. I had intended to make a statement when the negotiations, which are now pending, were completed, and to lay the papers on the table of the House then ; but, as the matter has been mentioned. I desire to say that it is true that Canada, a short time ago, renewed the offer which was made to the Imperial government as long ago as 1902, at the time of the colonial conference, to relieve the mother country from all expenditure in maintaining the garrisons of Halifax and Esquimau, and that the offer has been gladly accepted by the Imperial authorities. Correspondence is now going on and negotiations pending by which the transfer can be carried out. The principles upon which this transfer is to be made are these : First, that the Dominion government shall con-Mr. SAM. HUGHES.
trol these garrisons, and secondly that the Dominion government shall bear all the expenditure connected with maintaining them. In 1902, as I have said, in the papers which were exchanged between the government and the Colonial Office, and which form part of the papers which have been laid on the table of the House, giving the details of what took place at the colonial conference, it was stated in general terms-and there can be no doubt as to the meaning-that while Canada was not able to accept the suggestions of the' Imperial government-the War Office and the Admiralty particularly-as to the method by which Canada would aid in the defence of the empire, the government and people of Canada would be desirous of relieving the Britsh tax-payer, so far as that could possibly be done, and it seemed to the government, as I am sure it will appear to the people of this country, that obviously the first way in which that could be done would be by relieving the mother country from expenditure on Canadian territory. I will only make a single allusion to what my hon. friend said, and I am sorry that he differs from my views in this matter. I believe he will find that he is differing from the views of a large majority of the people of this country. My hon. friend, while he is not willing to take over the responsibility for the expenditure in connection with the garrisons at Halifax and Esquimau, wishes to send troops to Malta and other places outside of the country. Let me say to my hon. friend that charity begins at home. Let us discharge our responsibilities within our own borders first. I hope, during the present session, at any rate, to be able to lay all the papers connected with this matter upon the table of the House.

Before the hon. gentleman (Sir Frederick Borden) sits down, I woud like to ask him one question. It will be more convenient, of course, to discuss the question fully when the papers are brought down. Will these two ports. Esquimau and Halifax, be maintained in the same state of efficiency as they have in the past as far as the fortifications are concerned ?	'
Probably so.

It has been suggested, as far as Halifax is concerned, that the main reason for maintaining the fortifications which exist there at the present time is the fact that Halifax is a naval base for the North Atlantic squadron. If it is not to be a naval base in the future, will that modify the' attitude of the government in regard to these fortifications, or is there any probability that, although it is not intended in the immediate future that it shall be retained as a naval base, the policy which apparently has been entered upon by

the Imperial government in that regard may in the future be modified ? I have heard suggestions along both of these lines from gentlemen who ought to be pretty well informed on the subject, and possibly the hon. minister, without discussing the matter very fully, can give the House some statement as to what the future is to be in that regard in connection with these two points.

I regret that I am not sufficiently well informed to answer that question, but I may say to my hon. friend that, so far as the negotiations have gone, there is no indication of any intention on the part of the British government to abandon Halifax as a naval base.
But have they not dismantled the dockyard ?
Well, they have removed some men from there but I do not think they have dismantled it in that sense. I think it is to be continued as a naval base.
I had a different impression. However, the hon. gentleman (Sir Frederick Borden) may be right.

Before you leave the chair, I would like to ask the Postmaster General (Sir William Mulock) who is leading the House in the absence of the hon. the Prime Minister, to give, not to-night but at some future date, information to the House with regard to a certain matter affecting recent elections in some constitu-eices of Canada. If the hon. gentleman will refer to section 21 of the Dominion Elections Act, 1900, he will observe that it is therein provided that :
Immediately after the issue of the writ of election the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery shall transmit to the returning officer a sufficient number of copies of voters' lists, if there are any, one copy of this Act and of such instructions approved by the Governor in Council as are required to carry out the election according to the provisions of this Act

That is the important part of it. a sufficient number of copies of the voters' lists.
By another provision of the same Act which is to be found in section 92 subsection 3 and which deals with the duties of the returning officer after the election it is provided that:
The returning officer shall also transmit to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery the writ, With his return, the stamp furnished him for stamping the ballot papers and all the ballot papers, including those unused, the original statements of the several deputy returning officers, hereinbefore referred to, together with the lists of voters and poll-books, used in the several polling divisions.
The Postmaster General will observe that, in short, there is a direction to the Clerk of
the Crown in Chancery to forward to the returning officer a sufficient number of copies of the voters' lists and a further direction to him, after the election has been completed, to return to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery the voters' lists that have just been used in the several polling divisions. It has been a matter of public notoriety and the circumstances >
has, as I understand, been disclosed in judicial proceedings in Manitoba, that the voters' lists which should have been returned to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery by the several returning officers have not been so returned, or at least they are not forthcoming, although they have been required under subpoena and by the ordinary process of law in proceedings in Manitoba. I would like information from the government as to whether or not all the voters' lists so used in the several polling districts in the electoral divisions of Brandon, Lisgar, Marquette, Macdonald, Proveneher, Portage la Prairie, Selkirk and Souris, have been returned to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery. I would like also any information which may be in the possession of the government as to the reasons for any difficulty w'hich has occurred in procuring for production in evidence these documents which should have been returned by tfie returning officers to whom I have alluded. I thought this matter of sufficient importance to justify me in bringing this subject to the attention of the government in this way because these officials, as is well understood, are officers of this House. They are bound to obey the provisions of the statute to which I have referred and if through any malfeasance, or indeed through any unintentional dereliction of duty, through carelessness merely, they have not returned these lists as they were bound to do under the law. it may be necessary that some notice of that circumstance by appropriate means should be taken by this House at a later day.	.
I shall call the attention of the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) to the remarks of my hon. friend, and I have no doubt that he will give the information that is desired.

I am not desirous dn any way of placing myself on record as obstructing appropriations of any moneys necessary for the completion and proper equipment of the Sault Ste. Marie canal and its approaches. From time to time during the last five years at least these appropriations have been before the House. In 1900, $40,000 was appropriated, and in 1901 $100,000 was appropriated, to deepen and widen the entrance. In 1901 it was stated that the total cost of deepening and widening would be $450,000. This statement was repeated in
1902.	Again, in connection with the supplementary estimates for the same year, the estimate for the completion was $420,000. In 1902 $50,000 was appropriated, besides $20,000 in the supplementary estimates. In
1903,	$94,000 was appropriated, in 1904, $170-, 000, and we are now asked to appropriate $100,000. These make a grand total of $599,000, and the hon. minister says that will not complete the work. Will the hon. gentleman explain what circumstances or difficulties have arisen to have so far increased the cost ?

In the first place, there has been from time to time quite a variation with respect to the cost of the work. It has all been done by tender. The cost of dredging has varied from 80 cents to $3 per cubic yard.
What is $3 paid for ?
For rock dredging at the upper entrance.
Is $3 per yard paid for removing boulders ?

Yes, the contractors are obliged to take everything, whether solid rock, hard-pan, or whatever it may be. This same firm, Hickler Bros., had a contract for deepening the upper entrance or a portion of the upper entrance at the end of the Vidal <Shoal, and their price was 80 cents. We let another contract last fall for deepening another portion of the upper entrance, from the eastern end of the entrance to the eastern end of what is known as Vidal Shoal. The lowest tender for that was $1.74 per cubic yard. This was let to C. S.

Boone, of Toronto. We have some work at the south entrance pier, which is under contract to Mr. Birmingham, of Ottawa. We have expended on that up to the 30th of November, 1904, $37,500.

Whenever these items are submitted to the House, the question is raised as to the utility of this canal, and that question seems to resolve itself under two headings. First,' as to whether the fact that the canal is not being used as much as the American one, is due to the difficulty, in getting supplies or to the lack of dock accommodation on the Canadian side. I wish to draw to the attention of the hon. minister the present condition of affairs. It is true that when last this appropriation was asked for, it was stated that the government dock was then in course of construction. That dock has since been completed, but I might point out that it is some distance below the canal and does not seem to have remedied the condition of affairs. It seems that the Canadian Pacific Railway boats prefer, in coming down from the west or the north, to turn round and go to the American side rather than proceed along the shoally channel to where the new dock is situated. There is no doubt that between the eastern outlet of that canal and the present newly constructed government dock there is a channel difficult of navigation. It has repeatedly been represented to me that the captains of these Canadian Pacific Railway vessels will not follow that channel if they can avoid doing so. They invariably make a sharp detour to the south and go over to the American side. In 1902, when the appropriation was first asked for (see page 4002 of ' Hansard ') the then Minister of Railways and Canals used these words :
We desire to place our canal upon an equally satisfactory footing with that of our neighbours.
The footing of the canal proper is no doubt equally satisfactory to that of the American canal because when vessels go into the Canadian canal, they go into a better lock than the American, a lock which will serve vessels very [DOT]much quicker, which is in many respects a superior lock and under excellent management. But the difficulties are the difficulties of approach and the difficulties of docking. The difficulties of approach seem to have been grappled with to some extent by the large amount of dredging and deepening done, but I would point out that these difficulties have not been entirely removed although the expenditure has far exceeded the amount estimated. The difficulty of docking too is one that still calls for some consideration. The government dock is nearly a mile south of the entrance on the southern outlet of the canal, and there is in addition to the distance between the outlet and this government dock an unsatisfactory channel. I earnestly trust that the hon. minister will 45	k-16
investigate these matters as they stand. Speaking purely for the local constituency and having natural interest in the condition of affairs as they exist there by contrast with the condition of affairs existing at the American Soo, I would much prefer that the government should undertake to place our canal on an equally satisfactory footing with that of our neighbours from every point of view ; and the hon. minister will meet with no dissent from me if he will provide an amount sufficient to complete that work and place it on a satisfactory footing. Whilst speaking on this matter, I consider that the conditions which have prevailed with regard to these contracts on the canal call for some comment at my hands, and I regret that the Postmaster General, who is also the Minister of Labour, is not in his place.

Is this the contract referred to in answer to a question which I put on February 6. I asked :
1.	In what month in 1903 was the contract for dredging Sault1 Ste. Marie canal given ?
2.	If given in the fall, why was it given at a season when Canadian contractors were unable to take the work ?
3.	Did United States contractors get the work?
4.	What was the price ?
5.	Was there such a rush to have the work done that Canadian contractors were excluded from doing the work ?
The answer to the question was as follows :
1.	In November.
2.	It was given in the autumn because parliamentary appropriations were not available until then, parliament having prorogued on October 24. 1903.
3.	Yes.
4.	Eighty cents per cubic yard.
5.	It was necessary to let the work as early after the House prorogued to avail of the appropriation.
That contract was completed. This contract was entered into last autumn.

But, under this head, I dare say, I can refer to this for a moment. In answer to question 3, the minister states that the contractors who got the work were United States contractors. I suppose the reason they got the work was that tenders were called for late in the fall, when it was impossible for Canadian contractors to get their plant in place for the work. Consequently, the government are paying for the work double what they are paying on the Welland canal for a similar class of work. On the Welland canal they are paying 384 cents, while on the Sault Ste. Marie canal they are paying 80 cents a yard, as I understand it, for a similar class of excavation.
There is no comparison.
This is earth, not rock, excavation.
It includes boulders and hardpan. The work the Hickler Bros, are doing at 80 cents we are obliged to pay $1.74 for, and the offers made have been as high as $3.

I am advised by a very competent contractor that at the time the tenders were called for it was absolutely impossible for any Canadian contractor to put in a tender, because it was at a season of the year when it would have been impossible for them to get their plant there, and consequently Americans got the contract at higher prices. Were there any Canadian contractors tendering for this work ?

I was not then in the department, and am not prepared to answer that question off-hand. The appropriation having been passed late, the asking for tenders was late. The Canadian contractors tendered in 1904, and it seems to me they had equal opportunities to do so in 1903. My hon. friend (Mr. Pringle) is certainly misinformed as to the character of the work. It is absolutely different from the work on the Welland canal. I myself naturally asked the question why the tenders in connection with the Sault Ste. Marie canal were so much higher than those on the Welland canal, and so I was informed of the difference in the work. The successful tenderer last fall was Mr. Boone, whose figure was $1.74. Messrs. Magann & Finn, who are doing the work at 38i cents on the Welland canal, tendered at $2, and Messrs. Battle & Manley, tendered at $2.25. It is practically the same class of work. It was just at the entrance at the upper or northern end of the canal.

I am advised that the contract was let late in November, when very little if any work could be done, because the canal is usually frozen about the first week in December. The work would have to be held over until the spring, and there was no advantage in letting the contract so late in the fall, when only a few days' work could be done. If a reasonable time had been given our Canadian contractors would have had an opportpnity to bid for the work.

Though the work was given out late in the fall, the Canadian contractors were in quite as good a position to tender as those on the other side of the line. The point was to get the work under contract and have it ready to proceed with in the spring. It has been a crying necessity. Complaints were made that there was only 18 feet of water there, and it was said the Canadian Pacific Railway boats could not come down because of the shallow entrance to the canal. Another objection was the cross-current which was said to make the shallow water much more dangerous. The Mr. EMMERSON.
money, no doubt, should have ben voted earlier in the session, but we all recognize the conditions which prevailed here in 1903. The moment the vote was available tenders were asked for. The prices were certainly very low. And if, as the hon. gentleman says, no work was done that fall, surely the other contractors might have been quite as wide awake to the point as were Hickler Bros., the successful tenderers. Of course, we hear these rumours, but I think that when the facts are inquired into no cause for complaint can be found. When it came down to last fall the tenders were sky-high. They did not offer to take the work at any such figure as 38 J cents a yard. And, by the way, somebody complained the other night that 38* cents was too nigh.
I may not correctly understand this matter, but, as I am advised, tenders were called for on this work, work to proceed in the fall of 1903.
Nobody is expected to do the impossible.

Tenders were not called for until such time as it would have been impossible for Canadian contractors to get their plant on the Sault Ste. Marie canal. As to the minister's excuse that there was no appropriation, we all know that in 1903 a special vote was passed early in the session, so that these public works could be carried on, and thus there was no reason why tenders should not have been called for early in that session instead of waiting until the fall. Now, so far as the cost of the work is concerned, I am not prepared to say.
I think that was on the main estimates, there was a certain percentage.

You could have done the same thing again. What was to prevent you from bringing down an interim estimate to carry on this work, instead of leaving it to the fall so as to throw this contract into the hands of these American contractors ?

That particular work was kept going, because I do not think it was under contract. As for the other work, I do not think any dredging was being done at that period.	.

As the Minister of Labour is now in his place I desire to draw his attention to the condition of affairs which has existed at that place, on both government contracts and other works of a large nature, with regard to the employment of aliens. The matter has been brought from time to time, with a great deal of pertinacity, to the attention of the Department of Labour, and absolutely no relief whatsoever has been afforded. Now, here you

have a dredge contract involving a large amount of money, with foreign contracts, a foreign dredge, manned by foreign engineers, supplied from a foreign port, and employing foreign workmen.
Are you sure ?

I am speaking from very excellent information, that notwithstanding the clause that may have been imported into the contract, as it was imported into a contract by the Public Works Department, these conditions do and did exist at the time, and complaint was made with regard to it. There were importations of labour from the other side of the river for the purpose of dredging and deepening this canal-that can be established. There were importations of cheap foreign labour for the construction of the government dock, and that can be established. There was a time last year when the post office work there was under construction, that the stonemasons employed at the work were almost entirely, as 1 am informed, engaged from the United States across the river. So that on the three public works that were going on under a contract with this government at the town of Sault Ste. Marie, although that contract provided as the minister states, that the contractor should employ none but Canadian labour, that clause was honoured more in the breach than in the observance. Then what was the effect upon the town ? We find that during this time, according to this estimable publication from the bureau of labour, there is a report from Sault Ste. Marie on the labour conditions there-X am referring to the number for July, 1904, which, I may state, was the month following the date on which urgent petitions were sent to the Minister of Labour from the labouring men and other persons asking for relief. In the month of July, 1904, this article or minute appeared in the ' Labour Gazette : '
Labour conditions in Sault Ste. Marie are at! present duller than at any previous period in the last seven years. There is a large number of men employed, yet there are many more here than the amount of work calls for.
Yet what work there was there was being filled up by aliens imported under a government contract by government contractors upon a government work.
The receiver, however, has as yet only three) plants in operation, viz., the mechanical pulp mill, employing 140 men ; the veneer mill, employing 100 men, and the sawmill, employing 100 men. The contractor who is extending the government dock has 25 men employed, at a rate from $1.50 to $2 per day. The contractors on the post office building employ 45 men at wages ranging from $1.75 to $4.50, and on the extension of the pier, on the eastern approach to the ship canal, 45 men were employed at daily wages ranging from $1.50 to $4.50.
That is the report in the month of July, and in the month of August not a single word was said with regard to the urgent
45*
petitions that were presented to the Department of Labour in this issue of July. So it would appear that the organ of that department desired to say smooth things instead of true things. Then in the month for August, I extract from the report from Sault Ste. Marie, page 165 :
Sixty men are employed on the extension of the piers of the government canal at from $1.50 to $2.50 per day. The men employed on the! post office building are as follows 6 stonemasons at 45 cents per hour ; 7 carpenters at 25 cents per hour ; 9 stone-cutters at 50 cents per hour ; 7 quarrymen at from $2.52 to $2.75 per day, and 20 labourers at from 17J to 20 cents per hour.
Then we are told that labour conditions in August had somewhat improved. The petitions that were sent down to the Department of Labour I would ask the minister, when it is convenient,' to lay on the table of the House. They set forth the grievances that then existed, namely, that Canadian workingmen were being ousted and being pushed on one side by importations of alien labour under a government contract. The result was that men in Canada, some of them owning property and paying taxes at the Canadian Soo, went over and endeavoured to obtain work in American factories on the Michigan side, with the result that the American officials deported them and sent them back with their chests of tools by the same ferry by which they came. These matters were, as X understand, represented by these petitions to the department and a request was made that an inspector be appointed under the Dominion Alien Labour law to retaliate against that kind of treatment, so that these gentlemen who were employed on government work and eating up the bread of Canadian citizens might be dealt with at least on the same basis as our Canadians were dealt with by American officials. There was a meeting held at the Soo at which I was present, and the gentleman who was the government candidate at the last election, was also present. This ques-tiop was put forcibly before us by a number of workingmen who were immediately affected by it, who represented the pros and the cons. The whole difficulty was discussed, and the government candidate at the last election stated-I think I am quoting his words fairly, I am sure I am desirous of doing so-stated that in his judgment the present law was unworkable, and he would see that pressure was brought to bear upon the government so that the conditions which were then presented to the meeting might be remedied.
Two instances were cited of the character I have mentioned of men living in Canada being deported by the American authorities with a number of cases where men were imported from the American Soo opposite, and were engaged upon the post office and other public works to which I have referred. These matters were represented to the D'e-

partment of Labour. A request was made for an inspector. No inspector for the enforcement of the labour law of Canada, as far as I know-if I am wrong the hon. minister will correct me-was appointed or is now on duty. The conditions there call for action, they call for the enforcement of some law even though it be enforcement by retaliation. Men there who own property and pay taxes-I am quoting from instances that came to my personal knowledge-are deprived of work. A man occupying the position of a stationary engineer, for instance, is pushed to one side and remains at home idle while a gentleman from the other side of the river who lives over there comes over and takes his work, brings his dinner pail over, eats his dinner, does his work and goes back to the southern side of the line at six o'clock and when wage day comes he carries his pay over there, while the man who fulfils the duties and bears the burdens of Canadian citizenship by the payment of taxation and in other ways is looking for work. This is an example of the way in which the Alien Labour Law is administered at the present time. I would respectfully ask the hon. minister whether he has dealt with the petitions which were presented and whether he intends in pursuance of the prayer of these petitions which were sent down last June to appoint an inspector and to carry into effect, as far as they can be made effective, the provisions of the Alien Labour Law so as to prevent this condition of things in the future. I would also ask the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals if in regard to the same appropriations he would see to it that the clause in the contract for the expenditure of this money on this dredging and deepening work providing for the employment of Canadian labour is not a matter of mere form more honoured in the breach than in the observance.

I would say in reply to my hon. friend that if he is not more accurate in respect to the Department of Railways and Canals, I fear that he has not given us very correct information as respects the conditions at the Soo. I happen to know from an inquiry that was made by the Department of Railways and Canals that Hick-ler Bros, who had the contract and who were said to be American citizens and employed in their work aliens-
Yes, I understand so.

Inquiry was made at the time and there was only one man on each dredge who was an American citizen. That was the engineer and captain, and further inquiry was made and it was found that it was impossible to get on the Canadian side any one who would undertake that work.
May I ask the hon. minister at what time he made these inquiries ?

These inquiries were made in the spring of 1904. The contract was let in November, I think, 1903. I came into my department in January, 1904. My attention was called to the matter, and I asked the chief engineer to make inquiry and the result of that inquiry was as I have stated.
Mr. Chairman

I hope my hon. friend is not subject to any little fits of that kind ; jumping up and interrupting me. I am stating the facts as they are and if he will bear with me I will get them all placed before him. The results of the inquiry were that it was impossible to get any one to act in that capacity on these dredges and in view of these circumstances permission was given to the contractors to employ these men in the operation of the dredges. They did the work excellently well. All other employees in connection with the work were Canadian citizens, as they informed me.

At the risk of speaking too much, which, in the eyes of the hon. minister, appears to be a heinous offence, I want to say that if he will read my remarks as taken down by ' Hansard ' he will see that the meeting I referred to was held in June of this year at which certain instances were brought to the attention of the meeting. He is groping away back in January of last year when everything was frozen up and I do not think anything was working. The hon. gentleman has referred in almost uncalled for manner to some desire on my part, possibly impulsively exhibited, of making myself right with him in regard to the facts. I might discourse upon that enigmatical stare and inscrutable smile with which the hon. gentleman meets certain questions which are asked in regard to the expenditures of his department, but I refrain out of courtesy to the hon. gentleman. % But, although I am a new member I trust'I am not a fresh one, and I want to draw the hon. gentleman's attention to the fact that I have never violated my rights here, that I have kept strictly within the lines of courtesy and no one can complain of me on that score. I do not think when I am addressing myself to public questions that I should be subject to remarks and insinuations of that character from the hon. gentleman.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Boyce) stated that some petitions and communications had last year been addressed to the Department of Labour complaining of some infractions of the Alien Labour law at the Soo. If the hon. gentleman had informed me in advance, I should have examined the papers and put myself in a position to discuss what has occurred, or is supposed to have occurred, but as the hon. gentleman has not done so-

I am sure it was from inadvertence-I am not in a position to-night to enter into any controversy as to what might or might not have occurred. The hon. gentleman says there were infractions of the Alien Labour law and he asks whether an inspector has been sent up there, or will be, and why one is not sent. Let me remind him that the Alien Labour Act is not administered in that way at all. At one time it was for the government to administer the Alien Act, but, at the instance of I think, speaking from memory, the Congress of Labour,-although I would not say positively as to which organization it was,-but on the application of labour organizations, the law was changed and the administration taken from the Department of Justice. It was left to any private citizen to enforce the law. If the hon. gentleman had turned up the Act at that time and had found there were infractions of the law all he had to do was to have a complaint made to a judicial or semi-judicial officer at the Sault, or to have had proceedings instituted and that would have brought about the proper remedy. That has been done with great success in many parts of Canada.
But these proceedings would have to be undertaken at the expense of the prosecutor, some poor labouring man who has not a dollar.

The law is as we were asked to make it by the labour organizations, the persons supposed to be particularly interested in it. The law provides that the government give one-half the penalty recovered to the complainant; in every instance that has been done, and it has not been complained to us that there are not people there prepared to undertake a prosecution. If my hon. friend in his zeal to help the workmen, had given them the beueht of his legal knowledge-for I presume he knows the law-he would have applied the remedy and we would not have had the grievance dragged out at such length in this House.

I am grateful for the explanation. but I wish to point out this difficulty. The average workman does not see the profit to himself or the advisability or the expediency of engaging personally in litigation, engaging lawyers to pursue a claim for penalties and giving security for costs, with the gracious promise that he may get one-half the reward. We know that the result of penal actions is exceedingly hazardous, much more so than civil actions, for the construction of the statutes is so strict that in a very small percentage of cases that are instituted to recover penalties is the plaintiff successful. Then what is the chance of his recovering against aliens or against a class of men who stand between the contractor and the employer of alien labour ? There are many difficulties,
and. knowing as I do that the minister is familiar with the provisions of the Act, it is with exceeding diffidence that I bring these matters to his notice and respectfully urge that they receive the attention they should receive.

These are observations that would be properly addressed to the House in framing amendments to the law, but they have no application, no force, as against the existing law. It is not necessary to repeat that the enforcement of the penalties does not rest with the government and the government has no legal right to institute proceedings such as the hon. gentleman refers to. We cannot by force of arms proceed to grab men and throw them out of the country. There is a legal way of doing these things. My hon. friend holds out the great bug-bear of security for costs. On referring to the Act he will not find anything in it with reference to security for costs there is nothing in the Act on the subject.
